Hey, it's Adrian! Uptober ended in the red for the second year in a row. Bitcoin fell 7.2% in October, and on top of that North Korea drained $6.3 billion from Binance, the biggest hack in crypto history. Not exactly the month the brochure promised. Last week I asked whether crypto would go down if stocks get a proper correction. October answered it: When the AI trade cracked, Bitcoin fell harder than the S&P 500, together with gold and silver. Though look at what happened after the hack. Bitcoin dipped to $76.1k, right into the 50-week moving average I said I expected to hold, and Binance made its users whole within three days. Then the Democrats took both the House and the Senate on Tuesday, and Bitcoin squeezed back above $80k. It didn’t last long. On Thursday the Nasdaq fell about 4% on new AI fears, and Bitcoin went right back down with it. As I write, it sits at $75.9k, exactly on the 50-week moving average again. So does my early bull call need to be revisited? Not yet. It’s being tested a second time this week, and Sunday’s weekly close is the one that counts. Caption: 

# Thursday links: Could prediction markets do more than predict?

[Kalshi: Markets beat models](https://kalshi.com/research/kalshi-research-midterms-calibration-and-accuracy.pdf)

A Kalshi research report reviewing the recent performance of prediction markets has determined they did a great job. In the midterms, Kalshi’s market-based probabilities were more accurate than either traditional polls or the forecasting models based on polls.

“Kalshi matched or exceeded polling averages at every horizon where they existed, and on the 9 am Election Day snapshot recorded the lowest Brier score of all forecasts compared,” the report concluded.

(In related news, I have reviewed my recent job performance and determined I deserve a raise.)

“Brier score” is a statistical method of judging the accuracy of probabilistic forecasts and lower scores are better. They’re calculated as the squared difference between the forecasted probability of an event occurring and the event’s actual outcome.

This penalizes overconfidence. For example, assigning a 90% probability to something that _doesn’t_ happen gives you a high Brier score: (0.9 − 0)^2^ = 0.81.  Assigning a 90% probability to something that _does_ happen gives you a very low one (0.9 − 1)^2^ = 0.01. 

Kalshi says its Brier score is the lowest:

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b33b216a-f795-4be2-88db-d9bf3759025f/image.jpeg?t=1793918497)
Caption: 

A perfect Brier score is 0 (no difference between predictions and outcomes), so 0.014 is very, very good.

On that metric, at least, Kalshi’s markets beat Nate Silver’s models.

[Silver: Models beat markets](https://www.natesilver.net/p/models-led-prediction-markets-in?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=1198116&post
